title: Prompt-to-Task Workshop (Lab)
summary: Students tackle a richer multi-requirement task with two different prompt structures, compare them on completion and accuracy, and turn the stronger one into a reusable template with a verification step and risk check built in.
objectives: Complete a second, richer task and compare which prompt structure worked better.
Design a reusable prompt structure for a class of tasks.
Evaluate the outputs for accuracy and run a basic risk check.

sections.heading: Prompt-to-Task Workshop (Lab)
body: You can structure one prompt - now build something reusable. Today you compare prompt structures on a richer task and design a template you and your class can use again and again.

sections.heading: I can…
items: I can complete a richer task with a structured prompt and compare two structures.
I can design a reusable prompt template for similar tasks.
I can check an output for accuracy and complete a risk check.

terms.definition: A task with several requirements to complete.
The order and parts of a prompt, such as Goal-Context-Format.
A prompt skeleton with slots that works for many similar tasks.
Checking an output against a reliable source.
A quick check for personal data and possible errors.

sections.heading: Compare, then reuse
body: A [[richer task]] has several requirements, so a weak prompt structure leaves parts unfinished. Run two structures on the same task and compare which completes it and which is more accurate.
Then turn the winner into a [[reusable template]] - a prompt with labelled slots you can fill in for any similar task.

sections.heading: Build in the checks
body: Every good template forces two checks: verify the output against a reliable source, and run a [[risk check]] for personal data and errors.
This is how real AI solutions are designed - and it is the foundation for your signature activity in the coming weeks.

sections.label: Let's try it - hands-on
sections.heading: Let's try it - hands-on
body: Complete a richer task with two structures, compare them, then design a reusable template with checks built in.
items: List the three requirements of the task.
Draft two structured prompts with different orders.
Compare which output completed the task and check accuracy.
Turn the stronger structure into a reusable template.
Add a verification step and a risk check.

sections.heading: Think about it
items: Which structure completed more of the task, and how do you know?
Where should the verify step sit in your template?

sections.heading: My reflection
items: Write the biggest difference between your two structures.
Write how your template forces an accuracy check.

questions.prompt: The task had three requirements: name three school clubs, give the start time, and use a friendly tone. Structure A produced six lines that named three clubs, gave the start time and sounded friendly - but one club it named closed last year. Structure B produced twelve detailed lines, named two clubs, gave no start time and sounded friendly. Which judgement is the strongest?

options.text: Structure B is stronger because it gave far more detail than Structure A.
Structure A is stronger on completion, but its club list must be corrected after checking the school's club page.
Structure A is stronger, and because it met all three requirements there is nothing left to check.
Neither is stronger, because each output has a problem of some kind.

feedback.correct: You compared on completion and on accuracy: A met all three requirements, and the wrong club name is a fault to fix by verifying, not a reason to prefer the longer output.
feedback.incorrect: More words is not more complete, and meeting every requirement still does not prove the facts are right - judge completion first, then verify the winner against a reliable source.

questions.prompt: Which features make a prompt a reusable template rather than a one-off prompt? Choose all that apply.

options.text: It uses labelled slots such as 'Goal: [task]' that you fill in for each new task.
It ends with a step that checks the output against a reliable source.
It tells you to keep personal data out of the context.
It is longer and uses more words than a one-off prompt.
It names the exact topic of the first task you used it for.

feedback.correct: Slots let the template travel to new tasks, and the built-in verify and risk checks are what stop it being reused carelessly.
feedback.incorrect: A template is reusable because of its slots and its built-in checks - extra length adds nothing, and naming one task's topic locks the template to that task.

questions.prompt: Put the steps of the workshop in the order that lets you compare fairly and end with a template you can trust.

items.text: List the requirements the task has to meet.
Draft two prompts that use different structures.
Run both and mark which requirements each output met.
Check the facts in the stronger output against a reliable source.
Turn the stronger structure into a template with labelled slots and a verify step.

feedback.correct: The requirements come first because they are what you mark both structures against, and you only build a template out of a structure you have checked for accuracy.
feedback.incorrect: You need the requirements before you can say which structure completed more, and you should not turn a structure into a template until its output has survived an accuracy check.

questions.prompt: Complete the sentence about your template: A reusable template uses labelled ___ so the same skeleton fits many similar tasks, and it finishes with a step that tells you to ___ the output against a reliable source.

feedback.correct: Slots make the template reusable and the verify step makes it safe to reuse - a template without one is only half a template.
feedback.incorrect: A template needs both halves: labelled slots you fill in for each task, and a final instruction to verify the output against a reliable source.

questions.prompt: True or false: once your template has worked well on one task, you can use its output on a different task without checking it.

feedback.correct: Right - a template is a strong starting point, not a guarantee, so every new task still needs its output verified and risk-checked.
feedback.incorrect: A template that worked once only makes a good output more likely; the verify and risk steps are built in precisely because each new task can still go wrong.

formative.targets: Extends 'uses AI tools with structured prompts to complete tasks' toward reusable, evaluated solutions
formative.check: A reusable prompt template plus a comparison of two structures with accuracy checks
formative.successCriteria: Compares two structures on completion and accuracy and designs a reusable template with a verification step.
formative.evidence: Comparison notes and the reusable template with its risk check.
